title: tu and Lei: informal and formal you
rule: Tu with friends, family, children and peers who offer it; Lei with strangers, older people, officials and anyone with a title. Lei takes third-person verb forms.

items.n: Let's use tu with each other!

items.note: polite way to ask; the capital L is the formal pronoun

items.t: Buongiorno, dottoressa. Lei è di qui?
items.n: Good morning, doctor. Are you from here?

blocks.title: In the south
blocks.text: In parts of southern Italy, older people may use [[voi]] as a formal singular, a habit from the past: [[Voi siete il nipote di Cosimo?]] Understand it as Lei; answer with Lei.

blocks.title: The direction of politeness
blocks.text: Using Lei with someone who expects tu sounds cold but is never rude. Using tu with someone who expects Lei can be. When unsure, start with Lei; the other person will fix it in one sentence.

items.why: Ciao is informal; a title calls for the formal greeting.

items.wrong: Scusa, signora, Lei è la signora Caputo?
items.right: Scusi, signora, Lei è la signora Caputo?
items.why: Keep the register consistent: scusi with Lei.

items.q: Pasquale, 72, retired teacher, first meeting. You ask his name:
items.why: Lei with a stranger and a title.

items.q: Dora: «Dammi del tu!» — {hero}: «Va bene. Dora, ___ di qui?»
items.n: Dora: "Call me tu!" — {hero}: "All right. Dora, are you from here?"

items.q: Excuse me (formal), are you Italian? (to a woman)
